bread-white-with-whole-wheat-swirl-toast.title: Bread, white with whole wheat swirl, toasted

content.title: About
content.content: Bread, white with whole wheat swirl, toasted is a white loaf that incorporates a swirl of whole wheat dough and is then sliced and toasted to a golden crust. It has a soft, slightly sweet crumb, a toasted grain aroma, and a crunchy exterior.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional white bread is often enriched with whole‑grain additions to boost its nutritional value.
Toasting the slices enhances flavor and creates a satisfying crunch, especially popular in sandwiches.
The whole‑wheat swirl adds a visual accent, a nutty taste, and a modest amount of fiber.
In some cultures this bread is served with butter and honey as a classic breakfast.
The dough is usually given a longer fermentation to develop aroma and gluten structure.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: The bread provides steady energy through slowly digestible carbs, helping maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains whole grains
items.content: The whole‑wheat swirl adds fiber, B‑vitamins, and minerals such as iron and magnesium.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from the whole‑grain swirl promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many baked goods, this bread is low in fat when eaten plain.

items.title: Provides plant protein
items.content: Wheat bread supplies plant‑based protein important for tissue repair.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat bread contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White bread can raise blood sugar quickly, so individuals with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some commercial versions contain added salt; those watching sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Store‑bought loaves may include preservatives to extend shelf life.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Toasted slices are perfect for sandwiches, avocado toast, cheese, or pâtés. They can be used as croutons, breadcrumb bases for casseroles, or served alongside soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the bread in a cool, dry place in a paper bag or bread box. For longer storage, freeze slices in an airtight bag and toast as needed.

chicken-with-rice-and-vegetable-diet-fro.title: Chicken with Rice and Vegetables (Diet Frozen Meal)

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken with rice and vegetables is a diet frozen meal designed for convenient, balanced nutrition. It contains lean chicken breast, boiled rice, and a mix of vegetables (carrot, broccoli, peas). The meal is ready to eat after heating in a microwave or on the stovetop.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The meal provides about 250 kcal per serving, making it suitable for weight management.
Chicken is a high‑quality source of lean protein that supports muscle maintenance.
Rice supplies quick‑release carbohydrates, while vegetables add fiber and vitamins.
Flash‑freezing preserves most nutrients by rapidly lowering the temperature after cooking.
The product contains no added sugars or artificial colorings.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken breast delivers roughly 20 g of protein per serving, promoting satiety and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The meal contains less than 5 g of fat, primarily polyunsaturated fats that are heart‑friendly.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Rice provides steady energy without causing sharp blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Vegetables contribute vitamin C, vitamin A, potassium, and folate, supporting immunity and metabolism.

items.title: Supports weight control
items.content: A balanced ratio of protein, carbs, and fat makes the dish suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to poultry should avoid this product.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The meal contains a moderate amount of salt; those on low‑sodium diets should account for it.

items.title: Must be fully heated
items.content: Insufficient heating may leave live bacteria, increasing the risk of foodborne illness.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Some versions may include sauces with gluten; check the label if you have celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the meal in the microwave for 3–4 minutes or on the stovetop until it reaches 75 °C, then stir. Optionally garnish with fresh herbs or a drizzle of olive oil for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen product at –18 °C or lower. After thawing, consume within 24 hours and store in the refrigerator for no more than 2 days. Do not refreeze.

content.title: About
content.content: A chocolate‑covered marshmallow cookie is a crisp biscuit coated with milk or dark chocolate and dotted with soft marshmallow pieces. The blend of sweet chocolate, fluffy marshmallow and aromatic dough makes it a favorite treat for both kids and adults.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first versions appeared in the United States in the 1970s as part of confectionery experiments.
Traditional marshmallows were originally made from the root of the marshmallow plant, but today gelatin or vegan alternatives are used.
The chocolate coating helps keep the marshmallow pieces moist, preventing them from drying out.
The cookie is often used as a base for dessert tartlets and ice‑cream sundaes.
In some countries it is considered a seasonal snack for Halloween.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Sugars and carbohydrates provide quick replenishment of glycogen stores, delivering an immediate energy boost.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Dark chocolate is rich in flavonoids that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Mood support
items.content: Chocolate stimulates the production of serotonin and endorphins, which can improve mood.

items.title: Protein content
items.content: Both the biscuit dough and marshmallow contribute a modest amount of plant‑based protein useful for tissue repair.

items.title: Calcium from milk chocolate
items.content: Milk chocolate adds a small amount of calcium that supports bone health.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of cavities.

items.title: Allergy to dairy and gluten
items.content: Chocolate and the cookie base often contain milk and wheat, which may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: These cookies are calorie‑dense; moderation is recommended.

items.title: Possible trans fats
items.content: Some chocolate coatings may contain partially hydrogenated oils.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the cookie as a snack, crumble it over ice cream, use it in dessert parfaits, or stir it into yogurt. For a softer texture, gently warm it in the microwave so the chocolate becomes more fluid.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cookies in an airtight container at room temperature, away from direct sunlight. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator, though the chocolate may harden. Discard any cookies with off‑odors or signs of mold.

content.title: About
content.content: Miso is a traditional Japanese paste made by fermenting soybeans with salt and rice, barley, or other grains. It has a rich umami flavor that ranges from light and sweet to dark and salty, depending on fermentation time and ingredients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The earliest records of miso date back to the 8th century, with its predecessor being a Chinese soybean paste.
Main types of miso include white (shiro miso), yellow (shinshu miso) and red (aka miso).
Miso is commonly used as a base for soups, marinades, and sauces.
Fermentation can last from a few weeks to several years, influencing color and aroma.
In Japan miso is considered a “superfood” that supports digestion thanks to its probiotics.

items.title: Rich in probiotics
items.content: Fermentation creates beneficial bacteria that help maintain a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Source of protein and B‑vitamins
items.content: Miso provides plant‑based protein along with vitamins B2, B6 and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: It supplies iron, magnesium, zinc and copper, which are essential for bone health and immunity.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Fermented soy products have antioxidant activity that helps combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Studies suggest regular miso consumption may help lower cholesterol levels.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Miso is salty; people with hypertension should limit their intake.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to soy may experience reactions, up to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Additive concerns
items.content: Some commercial miso varieties may contain preservatives or flavor enhancers that are not suitable for everyone.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Miso is typically dissolved in hot (but not boiling) water and added to soups, sauces, marinades, and salad dressings. It can also be used as a base for stews, mixed into vegetable dishes, or blended with butter for a spread on toast.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store miso in an airtight container in the refrigerator. Properly kept, it retains flavor and quality for up to a year. Discard if mold appears or the smell becomes off.
